title: The pull home
hookLine: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, homesick for his bride

cards: First semester away. The new place is supposed to be the start of everything, and the student lying awake can only think about the kitchen at home, the dog, someone's voice saying come back soon.
Nanda had his own version of that. He was the Buddha's half-brother, the son of Mahapajapati, and he had become a monk. But one day he tells the other monks: I'm not happy living this life.
I can't keep it up. I'm going to give up the training and go back. Why?

teach.b: When I left home, Nanda tells the Buddha, a Sakyan girl, the loveliest in the land, looked up at me with her hair half combed and said: come back soon, master. I keep remembering it.
What the Buddha does next is startling.
He takes Nanda by the arm and, the text says, as easily as a strong man bends his arm, the two vanish and appear in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. There Nanda sees five hundred heavenly nymphs.
Which is lovelier, the Buddha asks, the Sakyan girl or these? Next to these, Nanda says, she's nothing at all. Then practice, the Buddha says, and I promise you these.
But the other monks hear about the deal and tease him: Nanda the hired hand, Nanda working for wages. Ashamed, Nanda goes off alone and practices in earnest.
And somewhere in that practice, the wanting itself falls away, both the girl and the nymphs.

teach.h: I RELEASE YOU FROM YOUR PROMISE.
teach.b: He goes back to the Buddha and says: I release you from your promise. I already knew, the Buddha says. The verse praises one who has crossed the mud of sense-desire and is no longer shaken by pleasure or pain.
Some readers take the story as a bigger desire used to loosen a smaller one, until both drop away.
And the ending is plain in the text: the pull wasn't beaten by force. It simply stopped pulling.

how: Nanda's story is often told in Buddhist communities, and in the Anguttara Nikaya Nanda is named foremost among monks in guarding the senses, the discipline he came to after his struggle.

the Buddha's half-brother, a homesick monk

Nanda overcame his longing by forcing himself to forget her
after the teasing he practiced in earnest, and the wanting itself fell away.
Nanda released the Buddha from his promise
once free, he no longer wanted the nymphs either.

games.q: you're Nanda. the other monks are mocking you for practicing just to win heavenly nymphs. what do you do?
o: leave the order and go home.
go off alone and practice in earnest.
games.why: ashamed, he withdraws and practices seriously, and reaches the end of craving. then he releases the Buddha from the promise.

practice: Ask gently what tugs at you when you try to keep a good intention: a habit, a person, a comfort, a picture in your head.
Let it come, the way Nanda's memory came, and without fighting it or following it, feel where the pull lives in the body. Then rest with the breath, and notice that the pull, too, rises and fades.

wordCard.voice: Nanda. The Buddha's half-brother, homesick for the girl he left, until the wanting itself fell away.

orig.note: Pali Nanda: a name meaning joy or delight.

carryVoice: Your line: it simply stopped pulling. Wanting rises and falls, like the breath. See you on day six hundred eighteen.
